item.title: PHP2Shell on NetScaler: to ASLR or not to ASLR?
item.description:
Yesterday anyone in IT will have followed the news about the two PHP bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, better known as PHP2Shell. I wrote a post on what they mean for Citrix NetScaler on the day the PHP fixes came out, before Citrix had released a statement.

Since then more information has come out. One thing I read is that triggering the bugs is the easy part. Turning them into code execution requires memory addresses, and those are normally hidden by ASLR (address space layout randomization). Most of the proof of concept exploits on GitHub don’t work at all. The ones that do either brute force the addresses or need a separate memory leak.

VulnCheck says the same, more on that below.

That made me look at what else NetScaler is built on. PHP 8.1 is not the only end of life component: NetScaler runs on FreeBSD 11.4, stripped down and customised by Citrix, and that has been end of life since 2021. Every FreeBSD version that is still supported has ASLR switched on by default. So I looked at two things: does ASLR really matter for these bugs, and does NetScaler have it?

Disclaimer: this is based on the PHP advisories and fix, public analysis and my own static analysis of the firmware (build 14.1-73.46). It is not confirmed by Citrix. I did not build an exploit and I won’t publish one.

item.title: Does PHP2Shell reach NetScaler? Taking the firmware apart to find out
item.description:
On 21 October 2026 PHP released fixes for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both pre-auth remote code execution and both CVSS 4.0 9.2. Public reporting calls the pair “PHP2Shell”. The worst case target in the advisories is Apache with mod_php.

NetScaler ships PHP as well. So the first questions from customers are easy to guess: which PHP version does NetScaler run, are we affected, where on the appliance does PHP actually run, and can it be reached from the internet?

This post is my answer for one firmware build, 14.1-73.46. The short version: yes, it is vulnerable, and I can show that in the disassembly, not just from a version number. But the vulnerable PHP only runs behind the management interface. The internet facing Gateway doesn’t reach it.

Disclaimer: until there is an official statement from Citrix, this is what I could determine from the public documentation and my own static analysis of the firmware. It is not confirmed by the vendor. Treat it as informed analysis, act on it carefully, and check it against the Citrix advisory once there is one.

Update 21 October 2026: a few hours after this post went live, Citrix published mitigation guidance. It confirms what I found: only the management interfaces are affected. See What Citrix says.

Update 22 October 2026: Citrix has published a security bulletin, CTX697263. It lists NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway as impacted and refers to the mitigation guidance above. There is no fixed build yet.

Update 22 October 2026: in a follow-up I looked at how exploitable this is on NetScaler, and whether NetScaler has ASLR. See PHP2Shell on NetScaler: to ASLR or not to ASLR?.

item.title: Blog improvements
item.description:
When I started this blog in 2007 (wow that’s almost 10 years ago) I went for a cheap web hoster with a reasonable performance to host it.

In the beginning performance was acceptable but over the years it has degraded and of course user experience standards have changed.

I decided it was time to do something about it so I’ve moved the blog from a shared platform to my own server.

This server is running on optimized flash storage  where most writes are DeDuplicated and never actually hits the flash disks:

item.title: Dumping passwords in a VMware .vmem file
item.description:
Benjamin Delpy the author of the well known mimikatz toolkit has released a very cool extension to WinDbg today.

In summary the extension can extract Windows passwords from memory dumps, hibernation files and Virtual Machine .vmem files (paging, snapshots).

Especially the ability to extract passwords from .vmem files was very interesting. So I decided to to test this out, so let's see how it works!

item.title: Bypassing RES/Appsense Application Security
item.description:
The video below shows a Proof of Concept of bypassing Application Security in RES Workspace Manager .

Please note that at this time the code is not publicly available so please don’t ask for it.

EDIT 2: I added a video that I received from someone who tried my Excel Sheet with AppSense Application Manager.

EDIT: I wanted to clarify a couple of things regarding this post.

First of all I would like to explain why I wrote this code and why I choose to test it with RES WM.

I had the idea about this approach a long time ago but I never got around to actually do it. The main reason was that I needed to convert Delphi code to VBA and especially converting some Windows headers was a lot of work. Then suddenly I noticed that someone had already converted the headers, so I all I had to do was rewrite the code that used it to VBA.

The choice for RES was made because of two reasons:

  1. If you want to beat something, you want to beat the best and I most certainly consider RES WM to be one of the top products.
  2. At the time I wrote the POC code I had access to an enviroment with RES in it.
I would like to emphasize that RES contacted me very quickly after publishing this blog. I've had contact with RES and they showed a very constructive approach with their primary goal being a fix or guidance for their customers. Hats of to RES taking a constructive approach and I will be working together with RES on this issue.

Finally I would like to state that I didn’t expect this post to draw this much attention, if I did I would have probably taken another approach.

item.title: Cross-Site Scripting Vulnerability in Citrix Web Interface
item.description:
from CTX127541:

A cross-site scripting vulnerability has been identified in specific versions of Citrix Web Interface.

This vulnerability could potentially be used to execute malicious client-side script in the same context as legitimate content from the web server; if this vulnerability is used to execute script in the browser of an authenticated user then the script may be able to gain access to the authenticated user’s session or other potentially sensitive information.
